# How to Train for a Hike on a Treadmill: An 8-Week Plan Built From Your Trail's Elevation


Last updated November 2026


On the steepest pitches, the Summit's hiking handles keep the incline and speed keys under your hands.


**Short answer:** To train for a hike on a treadmill, look up your trail's distance and elevation gain, then divide the feet gained per mile by 53. That's your treadmill incline. Spend 8 weeks building time at that grade, add intervals at the trail's steepest pitch, carry the pack you'll hike with, and practice walking downhill. Keep your grip on the rails as light as you can.


Famous hikes are less steep on average than most people think. Angels Landing, Half Dome and Mount Whitney all average between 10% and 13%, which almost any home treadmill can handle. They're hard for other reasons: 20% pitches hidden inside that average, hours on your feet, a loaded pack and a long walk back down. A treadmill plan can train for all of that if you build it from your trail's numbers.

## What Do You Need Before You Start?


- Your trail's total distance, total elevation gain and the grade of its steepest section. The park's trail page or the elevation profile on AllTrails has all three.
- A treadmill that reaches your trail's grade (Step 1 shows which ones do).
- The pack you'll actually carry. Water bottles make easy, adjustable weight.
- Eight weeks, with three treadmill sessions and two short strength sessions a week.
- Enough fitness to walk briskly for 30 minutes. If you're not there yet, add 2 to 4 weeks of easy walking first.


## Step 1: What Treadmill Incline Matches Your Trail?


Treadmill incline is a grade: feet of rise for every 100 feet forward. Trails are described in miles and feet of gain, so you need one conversion. Divide your trail's elevation gain by its one-way distance to get feet per mile, then divide that by 53. A trail that climbs 530 feet per mile averages about 10%.


On very steep trails the quick rule reads a little low. Here are the exact figures:

The averages hide the hard parts. The Upper Yosemite Falls trail averages 14.4%, but its first mile to Columbia Rock climbs 1,000 feet. That's a 19.3% grade, steeper than most home treadmills go. Check your trail's elevation profile for its steepest sustained section and write that grade down too.


Duration matters as much as grade. The Park Service says most hikers take around 4 hours for Angels Landing, and Whitney is a 22-mile round trip, so your legs have to keep climbing well into hour three. ## Step 2: How Much Climbing Is a Treadmill Workout Worth?


Hikers count vertical gain, so count it indoors too. Most treadmill displays show belt distance rather than vertical, so here are the approximate feet you climb in 60 minutes at common hiking speeds:


Incline 1.5 mph 2.0 mph 2.5 mph


10% 788 ft 1,051 ft 1,313 ft


15% 1,175 ft 1,566 ft 1,958 ft


20% 1,553 ft 2,071 ft 2,589 ft


30% 2,276 ft 3,034 ft 3,793 ft


42% 3,067 ft 4,089 ft 5,111 ft


Use it to size your sessions. Half Dome gains 4,800 feet. At 15% and 2 mph, matching that takes about three hours; at 30% and 1.5 mph, a little over two. The plan below splits that climbing across several sessions. On the Summit, top speed is capped at 6 mph above a 25.5% incline for safety, which is still far faster than anyone hikes a grade that steep.


An hour at 42% and 2 mph is about 4,100 feet of climbing, close to Half Dome's 4,800.


## Step 3: Follow the 8-Week Treadmill Hiking Plan


The plan uses three treadmill sessions a week, in line with[REI's advice](https://www.rei.com/learn/expert-advice/hiking-training.html) of three non-consecutive cardio days, plus two short strength sessions. Step-ups and lunges are the hiker staples. Every number comes from your trail:


- **Trail grade:** your trail's average grade from Step 1.
- **Steep grade:** its steepest sustained section.
- **Trail gain:** its total elevation gain.


Weeks Long climb (once a week) Other two sessions Downhill Pack


1 to 2: Base 45 to 60 min at trail grade 30 to 40 min at trail grade 5 min at -3% after the long climb None


3 to 4: Build 60 to 90 min, aiming for a third of your trail gain One easy 30 to 40 min; one with 5 x 3 min at steep grade, 2 min easy between 10 min at -6% 10% of body weight on the long climb


5 to 6: Trail-specific 90 to 120 min, aiming for half to two-thirds of your trail gain One easy; one with 6 x 4 min at steep grade 15 to 20 min at -6% Build up to trip weight


7: Dress rehearsal Two long climbs on back-to-back days that add up to your full trail gain One easy 30 min 20 min after each long climb Trip weight


8: Taper 45 min easy at trail grade One 30 min with 3 x 3 min at steep grade; then rest the 2 days before your hike 10 min Light or none


Do the long climbs at a pace where you can still talk in full sentences. During intervals you should only manage a few words at a time. If your steep grade is beyond what your treadmill can do, max out the incline and add pack weight instead.


You and your pack together have to stay under the treadmill's max user weight: 350 lb on the Summit and Podium, 300 lb on the Justice.


## Step 4: Should You Hold the Handrails?


As little as you can. In a[2006 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17135860/) , ten healthy adults aged 38 to 60 walked at the same speed and grade three different ways. At the hardest stage, gripping the handrails cut their oxygen uptake by about 21% and their heart rate by 21 beats per minute compared with swinging their arms freely. If you hang on tight, a 15% workout becomes a much easier one, and the trail won't have rails.


On the steepest settings, planting your hands is still the safe call. That's why the Summit's hiking handles carry the incline and speed keys and heart rate sensors: you can change the grade without letting go or reaching for the screen. Stay upright, keep your weight over your feet, and use the handles for balance rather than to pull yourself up. If you can only keep up by gripping hard, drop the grade or the speed. Whenever the grade allows, walk hands-free and swing your arms the way you will on the trail.


Stay upright, keep a light grip and let your feet carry the weight.


## Step 5: How Do You Train for the Downhill on a Treadmill?


Descents are where hiking legs fall apart. Walking downhill makes your quads brake with every step, and that braking work is what leaves you walking down stairs sideways the next day. The Bright Angel Trail opens with 4.5 miles and 3,040 feet of downhill before you climb a single step back out.


You can prepare for descents without wrecking your legs. In a[2016 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26920254/) , young men walked downhill on a treadmill at -28% carrying 10% of their body weight, once a week for four weeks. One group built up gradually, from 10 to 30, 50 and 70 minutes. They showed no signs of muscle damage, yet their eccentric knee extension strength still rose 19%. A group that started at 40 minutes had damaged muscles after the first session and ended up with a similar gain anyway. Ramp up your downhill minutes the same way and you get the strength without the wrecked legs.


Like most treadmills, the Justice and Podium start at 0%. The Summit drops to -6%. That's gentler than most trail descents, but it gives your quads regular braking practice, and Aviron's product page says the decline "lets you train descents too, which is what real terrain actually does and what most treadmills leave out." Do your decline minutes after the climb, when your legs are tired, as they will be on the trail. If your treadmill is flat-only, walk down stairs or a local hill instead, and add slow step-downs to your strength days.


## Which Treadmill Do You Need to Train for a Hike?


Match the machine to your trail's steepest section, not its average.


- **Summit (-6% to 42%):** the pick if your trail has pitches above 15 to 18%, or descents you want to train. It doesn't fold.
- **Podium (0 to 18%):** covers the average grade of every trail in the table above except the Manitou Incline, and it folds away. No decline.
- **Justice (0 to 15%):** fine for trails that stay under 15%, and the most compact of the three. No decline.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What incline on a treadmill is like hiking?


Many popular day hikes, including Angels Landing, Half Dome and Mount Whitney, average 10% to 13%, so that's a good place to start. Their steep sections often run 20% or more. To match a specific trail, divide its feet of gain per mile by 53. If you're new to incline, the[12-3-30 workout](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/12-3-30-treadmill-workout/) (12%, 3 mph, 30 minutes) is a quick test of where you stand.


### How long should you train for a hike?


Eight weeks is a solid runway for a big day hike if you already walk regularly. Give yourself 12 weeks or more for a multi-day trek, a heavy pack, or a start from zero. Either way, aim for three cardio sessions a week plus two short strength sessions.


### Is walking on an incline treadmill as good as hiking?


For your heart, lungs and climbing muscles, it's a very good substitute, and you can match the grade exactly. What it can't copy is uneven ground: rocks, roots, loose gravel and the balance they demand. Fill that gap with step-ups, lunges and single-leg balance work, and get onto a real trail or a long staircase a couple of times before the big day if you can.


### Is a StairMaster or an incline treadmill better for hiking?


Both build climbing legs. A stair machine suits stair-heavy trails like the Manitou Incline. An incline treadmill lets you match your trail's grade, carry your real pack and, if it has a decline, train the descent too. Our[StairMaster vs incline treadmill](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/stairmaster-vs-incline-treadmill/) comparison digs into the numbers.


### Can you train for altitude on a treadmill?


No. A treadmill builds the fitness for the climb, but not your body's adjustment to thinner air. That takes time at elevation. Even the City of Colorado Springs tells visitors coming from lower elevations to "allow your body to properly acclimate a few days before hiking the Incline."
